chapter_theme: Natrinai 0 to 20: an invocation that builds the discus-bearer's body from the cosmos, then poems across the five lands: hill girls guarding millet and hiding a first love, elopements seen by the lover as spring groves and by onlookers as a tiger's road, men who weigh wealth against a wife's gaze and stay, shore friends who press for marriage with gossip and threats of death, and a marutham wife who answers a husband's denial with an ironic portrait of the other woman; Ori's forest, Poraiyan's Thondi and Pazhaiyan's spear lend puram fame to private love.

0.reading: The invocation: they say that the god of the discus, who shines free of all harm, is the first lord of the Veda, whose feet are the great earth, whose garment is the sea where conches sound, whose body is the sky, whose hands are the quarters, whose eyes are the moon of cool rays with the sun, and who holds within himself all that has come to be.
0.nuance: The god is never named; he is known only by the discus (திகிரியோன்) and drawn as a body made of the cosmos, and the claim is put at one remove (என்ப, 'they say'), as if the poet reports the teaching of the Veda rather than a vision of his own.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து placed under paadaan

1.reading: The heroine answers the friend who told her he will leave: a man of steady word, sweeter the longer one knows him, he has never known how to part from her shoulders; the bond of the noble is high and pure like the sweet honey bees make from cool lotus pollen and store on a lofty sandal tree, and he, who graciously loves her because she cannot live without him as the world cannot live without water, fearing that her fragrant brow would pale, does not know how to do a mean thing.
1.nuance: Her proof is his character, not his promise: she reasons from what kind of man he is (நின்ற சொல்லர், புரையோர் கேண்மை) to what he cannot do. The honey simile carries the reasoning: a sweetness gathered from the low lotus and stored at the top of the hill tree, a bond made in one land and kept high in another. The world-and-water clause is the formula of Kural 20, bent here to her dependence on him.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்திய தோழிக்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: honey stored high on the hill sandal; no parting has happened, the bond is the matter

comparisons.vehicle: தாமரைத் தண் தாது ஊதி மீமிசைச் சாந்தில் தொடுத்த தீம் தேன்

comparisons.tenor: her, who cannot live without him

2.reading: Onlookers on the wasteland road, where in the bare forest of rustling date palms below a great cool hill the big-headed tiger cub, its head stained red and its mouth bloody from the travellers it struck down, eyes the deer at evening among the climbing iṇṭu and īṅkai, say that the youth who goes ahead of his sharp-toothed lovely girl through that country has a heart crueler than the thunder that, with wind-driven rain, shakes the great mountains.
2.nuance: The blame falls on the man alone, and its measure is a storm: beside the tiger cub's bloody evening the onlookers set a heart harder than mountain-shaking thunder, so the danger of the road and the youth's will are made the same kind of force. Line 1's அழுந்துபட and line 8's எல்லிடை (by night, or in the open light) leave the scene's time unsure.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகாநின்றாரை இடைச் சுரத்துக் கண்டார் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the bare wasteland road of an eloping couple

comparisons.vehicle: காலொடு பட்ட மாரி மால் வரை மிளிர்க்கும் உருமினும்

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the onlookers speak among themselves

3.reading: The man, whose heart again urges a journey for wealth, recalls an earlier one: at the strength-draining evening that met him at the edge of the wasteland, by a hot frontier hamlet of men whose plough is the bow, where under the dappled shade of a cracked-barked neem with sky-touching boughs, where the brooding kite cried, untaught children scratched a board like a gauge and played dice with gooseberries, did he not think of her, sweet as a finished task, at the hour she moves about the house with its fine lamp?
3.nuance: He likens her to the very thing the journey seeks, a task completed (வினை முடித்தன்ன), so the wife at home already is the success he would go out to win. The children's gooseberry game on the hot frontier pictures a home life he lacked at the hour it most mattered: evening, when the lamp is lit.

colophon.thurai: முன் ஒரு காலத்துப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hot frontier at the wasteland's edge, recalled from a journey for wealth

4.reading: With the man standing unseen nearby, the friend asks the heroine: if we tell the lord of the shore, where the fishermen of the grove hamlet rest in the rich shade of the dark punnai and dry their nets watching for the bright hour on the cool wide sea, that if mother learns of the gossip our life here will become hard, will he take us away to his own town on the dark backwater coast, where the roar of the salt-sellers' long-road carts, sunk in sand as they cry the sale of white crystal salt and rouse their herds, frightens the black-legged white heron in the fields?
4.nuance: The question is put so that he hears it, and its last image answers it: in his own town the clamour of the salt carts frightens even the heron of the fields, as the clamour of gossip frightens her here. The fishermen idling in the punnai shade while their nets dry is the leisure the lovers have had, now ending. Fear of the mother is entered as accham from இறை, the authority one lives under.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தோழி அலர் அச்சம் தோன்றச் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, punnai and nets of the seashore

occasion.words: அலர் அச்சம் தோன்றச் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

ullurai.tenor: the town's gossip and the girl it frightens

pairs.situation: the loud talk of the town about the secret love
the girl who fears that talk and her mother's hearing of it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the salt carts and the heron of the backwater, things of the poem's own neythal shore (porul 7.27)

5.reading: To the heroine, changed since she sensed the man's plan to leave, the friend says that even in this dewy season, when the clouds that have poured great rain thunder as they rise in the south, the land is soaked, the hills sprout, crops take root by the wide green pools and the fragrant creeper the hill-men cut sprouts again and twines round the sandal, it is hard for a lover to part; and the message her rain-heavy eyes have sent, with the north wind that brings back the young men setting out today, will hold him.
5.nuance: The poem never says he will stay; it lets the season argue (rain, sprouting, the cut creeper twining the sandal again) and calls her tears a தூது, an envoy, as if weeping were already a message he cannot ignore. The cut creeper that sprouts and winds round the sandal can be read as parted lovers rejoined, but it does no act of a person here, so it stays scene. The sense of lines 7 to 9 is unsure, and line 8 is a repaired line.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் செலவுக் குறிப்பு அறிந்து வேறுபட்ட தலைவிக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the matter is a parting to come; the hill and the rain are its setting

occasion.words: தலைவன் செலவுக் குறிப்பு அறிந்து வேறுபட்ட தலைவிக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

6.reading: The man, kept from the night meeting, tells his own heart within the friend's hearing that if he could find someone to go to the young girl, with skin like the tender stalk of the water lily stripped of its fibre, eyes like kuvalai and full shoulders, and tell her, she would not ask 'who is he?' but, she whose dark thick hair smells of the forest of Ori of the strong bow, where the bent ripe fruit of the kumizh by the path falls as food for the young deer, would be wholly overcome at hearing 'he has come'.
6.nuance: He does not doubt her love, only the means of reaching her: the speech is a wish for a messenger (செப்புநர்ப் பெறினே), and since it is said where the friend can hear, the wish is a request to her. Paranar gives the same pairing of Ori's forest and a girl's hair in Kuruntokai 199.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிப்பாற்பட்டு ஆற்றானாய தலைவன் தோழி கேட்ப தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a man in secret love seeking a way to reach her

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறிப்பாற்பட்டு ஆற்றானாய தலைவன் தோழி கேட்ப தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

7.reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose man has gone after wealth without marrying her, that the sky, roaring with its thunderbolts, is flashing to pour at once on the great forest of small-leaved sandal on the cool fragrant slope where the stripe-browed elephant that ate white paddy sleeps, while the spring in the wide god-haunted upland brims, waterfalls roar on the great slopes and the forest torrent, tumbling stones and drowning the bamboo, makes the woods resound.
7.nuance: The friend says nothing about him; she only announces the rains, and whether they comfort (the season he named for return has come) or alarm (the land he crosses is in flood) the poem leaves to the hearer. The fed elephant asleep on the cool slope is the one creature at rest in the storm; its ease, which she lacks, is a mood, not an act of the lovers, so it is scene.

colophon.thurai: பட்ட பின்றை வரையாது கிழவோன் நெட்டி இடைக் கழிந்து பொருள்வயிற் பிரிய ஆற்றாளாய தலைவிக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the friend points to the coming rains in a separation: the time of waiting

occasion.words: பட்ட பின்றை வரையாது கிழவோன் நெட்டி இடைக் கழிந்து பொருள்வயிற் பிரிய

8.reading: At the end of their first meeting, seeing her again among her companions, the man asks whose daughter she is, this simple girl with proud, red-lined rain-eyes that have known lingering longing, a leaf skirt of many flowers swaying at her waist and a body like a fine gem, who has brought him such pain; long live her father, and may the mother who bore her have the fortune of Thondi of Poraiyan of the strong chariots, where in the wide fields, even as reapers cut and binders carry, the eye-like neythal, spreading its strong stems through the cool mud, blooms in the stacked sheaves.
8.nuance: His first question is about her kin (யார் மகள்கொல்), and his first wish is a blessing on her father and mother, so desire already turns toward the family he will have to ask for her. The Thondi image is of fields so rich that flowers bloom in the cut stacks, a plenty that does not stop at harvest, and that is what he wishes on her mother.

colophon.thurai: இயற்கைப் புணர்ச்சி இறுதிக்கண் தலைமகளை ஆயத்தொடும் கண்ட தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a man struck by the girl at the end of their first meeting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; he speaks to himself

9.reading: Eloping with her, the man tells his white-toothed girl that, having won her soft bamboo-like shoulders so that his whirling distress is gone, as eager devotees who strive without fail see with their own eyes the god they worship, she may go without strain, rubbing the fire-bright young leaves of the flowering pungu on her lovely spotted breasts so that they hold a charm, lingering long at every shade and making sand dolls at every stretch of sand, for the road they take runs through forest of fragrant cool groves where the happy koel, pecking mango buds, calls, past many small villages.
9.nuance: The wasteland of the colophon is drawn as a spring garden and the journey as play (shade, sand dolls, leaves to rub on her breasts), so the man answers in advance the fear every elopement poem raises. Likening himself to devotees who at last see their god puts the girl in the god's place.

colophon.thurai: உடன்போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தலைமகட்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the lover leads the girl away on the road; elopement is paalai's matter even through a pleasant land

comparisons.vehicle: அழிவிலர் முயலும் ஆர்வ மாக்கள் வழிபடு தெய்வம் கண் கண்டாஅங்கு

10.reading: Handing over the girl as she elopes, the friend tells the man of the flowering town: even when her lifted lovely breasts sag and her fine long hair, hanging below the gems on her gold-like body, is bound up with grey, take care never to leave her, who has trusted your unfailing good word as one trusts the spear of Pazhaiyan, lord of Por of the white-tusked elephants, which struck true so that the victorious Cholas, of tall ornamented chariots and sweet strong toddy, could humble the Kongar.
10.nuance: The friend looks past the elopement to old age, naming the very changes (sagging breasts, grey hair) that might later be his excuse to leave, and binds him in advance. She holds him to his word with a war image: his promise must strike as surely as a famous spear, so his speech becomes a weapon he must answer for.

colophon.thurai: உடன்போக்கும் தோழி கையடுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the poem shows only the entrusting; the elopement comes from the colophon

11.reading: With the man standing unseen nearby, the friend tells the heroine, wilted in body like a garland left unworn since the signal he set failed her, to give up the resentful thought that he surely will not come: on the shore of flowered sand beaten by the waves the charioteer, sparing the crab beside the wheel's track, checks the reins as he drives, and the moonlight has spread over the seaside grove.
11.nuance: The answer to her doubt is a sound and a sight, not a promise: the chariot is already on the shore, driven slowly so as not to crush the crabs, and the moon is up. The care that spares a crab is the care he brings to her, though the poem leaves that unsaid; the crab is acted on, not acting, so it is not iraicchi. Lines 3 and 4 are compressed and their exact construction is unsure.

colophon.thurai: காப்பு மிகுதிக்கண் இடையீடுபட்டு ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகட்கு தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: crab, waves and the seaside grove

12.reading: The friend tells the man that at first dawn, when the worn churning stick, its rope frayed, roars at the post as it stirs out the ghee in the full-bellied pot that smells of wood-apple, the girl, hiding herself, slipped the pebble-filled anklets from her feet and set aside her finely striped ball as she went, saying 'whenever they see these my companions will grieve; pitiable, pitiable they are', and even as she eagerly made ready to come with you, her eyes wept beyond her control.
12.nuance: The report is meant to make him fear for her (the colophon's அஞ்சுவித்தது): her will is set but her eyes are not, and the things she leaves behind (anklets, the striped ball) are the things of girlhood her friends will find. Taking off the anklets, a rite of marriage, she does alone and in hiding while the house churns at dawn.

colophon.thurai: தோழி உடன்போக்கு அஞ்சுவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: a girl making ready to elope

13.reading: The friend, seeing the heroine changed the day after her first meeting and wanting her to hide it, says: you of the good great shoulders and red-lined rain-eyes like the arrows the millet-watchers pulled out after felling a beast, do not weep and spoil your beauty before strangers because the birds will not rise; the green-backed parrots that carry off the thick ears in the high hill glade, where vengai blossoms fall small and many like the sparks from gold a smith beats, know the peacock, it seems, and do not fear it.
13.nuance: The friend hands the girl an excuse to give out (the parrots will not leave the millet, so she weeps) to hide the real cause, her new love. The arrow simile is pointed: eyes red-streaked like arrows drawn bloody from a beast, a hunter's image for a girl who has just been struck herself. Lines 1 and 8 can be construed more than one way, so the excuse is uncertain in its detail.

colophon.thurai: இயற்கைப் புணர்ச்சியின் பிற்றை ஞான்று தலைவியின் வேறுபாடு கண்ட தோழி தலைவி மறைத்தற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: millet-guarding, vengai and parrots of the hill

comparisons.vehicle: ஏனல் காவலர் மா வீழ்த்துப் பறித்த பகழி

14.reading: To the friend who blamed the man, the heroine speaks for him: though he left without grace, her old beauty gone and her shoulders wasted, he will be gracious, for he loved her; though he went with gossip rising louder than the battle in which Sembiyan shattered Kuttuvan's Akappa and lit a fire by day, he has crossed the forest where fierce beasts roam, where on the kanthal slope, its great petals open and flowers bowed, the cry of a she-elephant, sleepless and afraid because the strong bull of her herd was seized by a python, echoes through the long mountain clefts.
14.nuance: She grants everything the friend says (the lost beauty, gossip loud as a war) and still affirms him; the comfort is her trust, not his return. The she-elephant crying for her mate on the road he crossed is a sound he too has heard.

colophon.thurai: இயற்பழித்த தோழிக்குத் தலைவி இயற்பட மொழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of a man gone across the wasteland

iraicchi.act: the she-elephant, sleepless with fear, cries through the clefts for her bull seized by a python
iraicchi.sense: the man who crossed that land has heard a mate grieving for its lost partner, and will remember the one he left

15.reading: Pressing the man to marry, the friend tells the lord of the shore of strong waters, where the north wind blows the huge dune the roaring waves heaped up into drifts like the ripple of fine cloth, that since we are not women you joined only to taste a flower-like beauty while it was new, we have held up our pledged heart as best we could, and, like a chaste young mother who lets her child go when a demon seizes it, have let go even the modesty that came with us from far back: let this town gossip.
15.nuance: The simile is the poem's force: modesty is given up as a faultless mother gives up her child to a demon, not by choice but to a power she cannot resist, so 'let the town talk' is defeat turned into a threat. The waves heap the dune and the wind scatters it; a reader may see his love and the talk that disperses it, but the poem anchors no such pairing, so the dune is scene.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட்டித்தவழி தோழி தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: waves, dune and shore

comparisons.vehicle: மாசு இல் கற்பின் மடவோள் குழவி பேஎய் வாங்கக் கைவிட்டாங்கு

occasion.words: வரைவு நீட்டித்தவழி தோழி தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

16.reading: The man, his heart set on a journey for wealth, gives it up: stay with her and wealth will not come, go after wealth and union will not stay; between these, my heart, whether you go or not you have a claim to the good; but wealth perishes like the trail of a fish darting through a pond of unwithering flowers, and even if I won a treasure measured seven times over with the wide wet world as the grain measure, I would have killed the sweet gentle look of her red-lined rain-eyes that suit her heavy earrings; let wealth be whatever it may.
16.nuance: The poem is a dilemma argued out, and the choice turns on what each side loses: wealth leaves no trace, like a fish's path in water, while going would destroy a look no measure of treasure could buy back. The world used as a grain measure makes the refusal absolute.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சினை நெருங்கித் தலைவன் செலவு அழுங்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: a journey for wealth weighed and given up

occasion.words: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சினை நெருங்கித் தலைவன் செலவு அழுங்கியது

17.reading: The heroine tells her friend, in words meant for others too, that when, gazing at the beauty lingering in the wide dark forest of the tall hill where the day's rain fell and the falls come down like the waves of the great sea, her lifted lovely rain-eyes wept, the water swirling and not stopping though she tried to hold it, her mother asked 'what have you done? let me kiss your shining teeth', and at such soft sweet words she nearly forgot the modesty dearer than life and almost said that what afflicted her was the chest of the man of the sky-touching hill, where the sapphire-coloured bee that sucked the kanthal on the slope hums like a sweet strung lute; she escaped saying it.
17.nuance: Kindness, not threat, nearly breaks her secret: the mother's tenderness is the danger. The bee that sucked the kanthal and now hums sweetly may be read as the man who enjoyed her and goes on content, but the poem gives only that one match, so it is a near miss for ullurai and stays scene. 'Modesty dearer than life' is the ranking the Tholkappiyam itself states.

colophon.thurai: முன்னிலைப்புறமொழியாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: falls, kanthal and the hill man

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: said to the friend so that another may hear; the colophon does not name who overhears

18.reading: The friend tells the heroine, unable to bear the parting, that he will come and the many sorrows of her troubled heart will leave: he crossed the hill whose single shining waterfall is like the lone tusk of a war elephant whose fury is spent after its must was washed off, in the war camp of Poraiyan of the victorious spear and unconquerable army, lord of Thondi of the seaside grove whose gate has Moovan's thorn-sharp teeth pressed into it, where the sleepless warriors who make hearts tremble sleep sweetly like a sea whose waves have stilled.
18.nuance: The whole picture is of rest after violence (an elephant calmed when its must is washed, warriors who never sleep sleeping like a stilled sea), so the friend wraps her promise of return in a war that is over. Moovan's teeth set in Thondi's gate are a war trophy remembered in a love poem.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைவியைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: comfort to a woman whose man has crossed the hills

comparisons.vehicle: கடாஅம் கழீஇய கதன் அடங்கு யானைத் தடாஅ நிலை ஒரு கோட்டன்ன

19.reading: To the man who has met her and is leaving, the friend says: lord of the shore of strong waters, where the thazhai with leaves thorny like a shark's horn, its rough bent trunk like a prawn's back and its buds ripening like a great tusker's tusks, stands out like a fine deer apart from the herd and fills the festival ground with scent, if you are going, your charioteer driving the tall chariot of clustered bells, then go, knowing well that she will not live through the few days until you come back.
19.nuance: The leave is granted only in form (செலீஇய சேறி ஆயின் ... சென்மே): 'go' brackets a sentence of death, which turns the farewell into a demand for marriage. The thazhai whose scent fills the festival ground is read by some as a love that can no longer stay hidden; the poem anchors no such pairing, so it is scene. Line 4's comparison is unsure.

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்து நீங்கிய தலைவனைத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: screwpine, shark and shore

occasion.words: புணர்ந்து நீங்கிய தலைவனைத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

20.reading: To the husband back from another woman who says he knows no one, the heroine says: sir, I saw the young girl; having passed the night asleep on the lord's chest, her hair fragrant with honey-dripping kadamba blossom, her gait swaying, her cloth fluttering, her tight bangles jingling as she swung her arms, she went off down the street turning her flower-like kohl eyes to look about, long may the girl live, wearing bright jewels over her many fine spots, her drooping earring crushed in the chest-to-chest embrace, her garland withered on shoulders where an old longing has settled, she who clung like a creeper.
20.nuance: She never accuses; she describes, and the description is the evidence (the crushed earring, the withered garland, a night on 'the lord's chest'), closed by a blessing (வாழிய மடந்தை) that is pure irony. The colophon's second reading gives the speech to the friend, but the address ஐய, 'sir', fits the husband better.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற்பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகன் யாரையும் அறியேன் என்றாற்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது வாயிலாகப் புக்க தோழிதலைவிக்குச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: a wife answering a husband's denial of another woman

occasion.words: பரத்தையிற்பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகன் யாரையும் அறியேன் என்றாற்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது

links.note: Natrinai 0 builds the discus-bearer's body from the cosmos: earth his feet, sea his garment, sky his body, the quarters his hands, moon and sun his eyes; Tirumanthiram 2774 gives Shiva the same map, space his body, the eight directions his hands, the three lights his three eyes, as he dances.
links.teaches: The body made of sky, quarters and heavenly lights is a frame older than either sect: the Sangam invocation fills it for the discus-bearer as a fact the Veda reports, and Tirumular fills it for Shiva and sets it dancing with a third eye of fire, so the image passed between gods while its parts stayed fixed.

links.note: Natrinai 1's heroine calls her man sweeter the longer one knows him (நீடுதோறு இனியர்) and the bond of the noble lofty; Kural 783 says the companionship of people of character delights the more it is practised, as a book does the more it is studied.
links.teaches: The heroine uses the Kural's rule about friendship with the noble as the premise of a love argument, reasoning from his character that he cannot leave her, so a maxim about good company served in akam as evidence against a report of parting.

links.note: Both use the formula of the world that cannot do without water (நீர் இன்று அமையா உலகம், நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு): Kural 20 as the first step of an argument that all conduct depends on rain, Natrinai 1 as the measure of how she cannot live without him.
links.teaches: The same clause is a step in Valluvar's proof about rain and a simile of a woman's dependence in Kapilar, which shows it was a common saying both drew on, apt to the akam poet for a lover's need as it was to the moralist for the world's.

links.note: Natrinai 2's onlookers see the elopement road as a wasteland where a tiger cub with blood on its mouth eyes deer at evening, and call the youth's heart crueler than thunder; in Natrinai 9 the eloping man describes the road as cool groves of koels and mango buds where she may linger in the shade and make sand dolls.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems give the same udanpokku road two natures by speaker, a tiger's evening for the bystanders and a spring garden for the lover, so the danger of paalai is a judgment the voices make and not only a fact of the land.

links.note: Both are Perumpathumanar's onlookers on an eloping pair: in Kuruntokai 7 they ask who these good, pitiable people are, the bowman and the girl with anklets still on, heading into the bamboo wilds; in Natrinai 2 they say the youth's heart is crueler than mountain-shaking thunder.
links.teaches: The same poet lets the onlookers pity both runaways in one poem and in the other lay the whole blame on the man who leads her into the tiger's country, so the kandor voice was a place to judge the hero, not only to witness the pair.

links.note: Both are a man answering a heart that urges a journey for wealth: in Natrinai 3 he recalls thinking of her at lamp-lighting time on the edge of the wasteland on an earlier journey; in Natrinai 16 he sets out the dilemma that wealth and union cannot both be had and gives up the journey.
links.teaches: The same refusal is reached once by memory and once by argument: Natrinai 3 calls her sweet as a finished task, putting the journey's goal already at home, and Natrinai 16 states the reason as a rule that wealth leaves no trace, so the decision is held both as felt experience and as reasoned principle.

links.note: Both concern the town's gossip about a secret love: Kural 1143's man asks whether gossip the whole town knows is not good for him, since it is like having what he has not yet got; Natrinai 4's friend fears that gossip reaching the mother will end the meetings and asks whether the man will take them to his own town.
links.teaches: The gossip that the Kural's man welcomes as a foretaste of union is, for the women of Natrinai 4, the danger that ends their meetings, which they can only turn into pressure to marry, so the worth of alar in the secret stage depends on who bears its cost.

links.note: Both name வல்வில் ஓரி: Purananuru 152 shows the hunter whose single arrow kills an elephant, a tiger, a stag, a boar and an iguana, and who feeds the bard venison; in Natrinai 6 the girl's hair smells of Ori's forest, where the ripe fruit of the kumizh falls as food for young deer.
links.teaches: The love poet takes from the hunter-patron's fame only his forest's scent and plenty, a place where the very deer his bow kills feed unharmed, so akam borrowed a puram name for the bounty of a land and left its violence behind.

links.note: Both are the man at first sight of the girl: Kural 1081 asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, his heart reeling; Natrinai 8 asks whose daughter she is, blesses her father and wishes on her mother the fortune of Thondi.
links.teaches: Valluvar's man asks what she is and the Natrinai man whose she is, his first words going to her parents, so the Sangam poem shows the couplet's stunned wonder already turning toward the kin and the marriage that will need them.

links.note: Natrinai 8 places in Poraiyan's Thondi neythal flowers that look like eyes; in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that beauty.
links.teaches: The Thondi neythal and a woman's eyes were a fixed pair that ran both ways, the flower measured by eyes in a man's first praise and the eyes by the flower in a woman's grief at separation, so one token marked beauty found and beauty lost at two stages of love.

links.note: Kuruntokai 7's onlookers see anklets still on the eloping girl's feet; in Natrinai 12 the friend tells how the girl, hiding herself at dawn, slipped off her pebble-filled anklets and left her striped ball before going.
links.teaches: Together they show the anklet as the mark of an unmarried girl, read by strangers on the road in one poem and taken off by the girl herself in secret in the other, so the eloping girl performs alone at dawn the change of state that a wedding would have made in public.

links.note: Both are about restraint that can no longer keep love hidden: Kural 1254's woman says she used to think herself restrained but her love now breaks out in public; Natrinai 15's friend tells the man they have let go even their long modesty and the town may gossip.
links.teaches: The Kural records the loss of restraint as an inner confession, while Natrinai 15 makes the same loss a threat spoken to the man, likened to a mother forced to give her child to a demon, so the collapse of naanam also served as a lever to force marriage.

links.note: Both hold that wealth does not stay: Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance and goes as it disperses; Natrinai 16 says wealth vanishes like the trail of a fish in a pond.
links.teaches: The Kural uses wealth's impermanence to counsel detachment, while the Natrinai man uses it to choose his wife's gaze over a journey, so the same doctrine served an argument for staying at home in love as well as one for letting go.

links.note: Both rank modesty above life: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for it but never shame for life; Natrinai 17's girl says she almost forgot the modesty dearer than life when her mother spoke softly.
links.teaches: The Kural states the ranking as a firm rule, and the Natrinai girl who holds it nearly breaks it not under threat but under a mother's tenderness, so the poem shows the rule's weak point to be a kindness the maxim does not foresee.

links.note: Both answer a lover's departure by saying she will not live until he returns: Kural 1151 says to tell his quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 19's friend says go, knowing well she will not live the few days till you come.
links.teaches: The couplet's bitter refusal of comfort appears in Natrinai 19 inside a friend's demand for marriage in the secret stage, so the claim that she will die before he returns worked in kalavu as pressure to marry and not only as grief.

links.note: Both are a wife's sulk at the husband's straying, fixed on his chest: Kural 1311 refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes; Natrinai 20 describes the girl who slept on the lord's chest and walked off at dawn with crushed earring and withered garland.
links.teaches: The Kural states the wife's charge in general terms, and Natrinai 20 shows the single scene behind such a charge, the rival's disordered body read as proof and blessed in irony, so the couplet's reproach rests on a convention of reading the other woman's appearance as evidence.

source_issues: 7: the colophon's நெட்டி இடைக் கழிந்து looks like a bad word division of நெட்டிடை கழிந்து (the colophon quotes the Tholkappiyam's phrase on a man who leaves for wealth without marrying); copied as it stands.
11: line 3 reads தௌளிதின், which looks like the TSCII fault flagged elsewhere (ௌ for ெள்), that is தெள்ளிதின்; not repaired in the core text.
5, 10, 20: repaired lines (5 line 8, 10 line 3, 20 line 5) as flagged by show; the readings follow the repaired text.
13: the construction of lines 1 and 8 (எழாஅ ஆகலின், மயில் அறிபு அறியா மன்னோ) is unsure, so the friend's excuse is uncertain in detail.
